stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When nutrition scientist Priya Valdés gave volunteers meals identical in calories but differing in how quickly they could be eaten, she expected little difference in later snacking. Instead, the observation that participants served the softer, faster-to-eat version of each meal—a puréed soup rather than chunky vegetables, for instance—reached for snacks sooner and ate more of them over the following three ______ Valdés to propose that eating speed, not calorie count alone, shapes fullness.
explanation: Remove the interruption between the dashes ("a puréed soup rather than chunky vegetables, for instance"). It already opens and closes, so nothing is left open. Next, find the main clause. Its subject is "the observation," and the clause starting with "that" tells you which observation: the one where participants "reached for snacks sooner and ate more of them over the following three hours." Those two verbs belong to the "that" clause. The main verb of the sentence is "led." So the blank sits between a very long subject and its verb, and a subject is never separated from its verb by punctuation. "Hours led" correctly gives you one sentence: the observation ... led Valdés to propose.

A.why: This is the breath-pause trap. The subject runs so long that a comma feels natural before "led," but no rule allows a comma between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is. If you took the comma as closing the "that" clause, notice that this clause identifies which observation is meant. It is essential, so nothing should mark where it ends.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "Led Valdés to propose..." has no subject of its own, and what comes before the semicolon is a subject with no main verb. You probably took "reached" and "ate" for the sentence's main verbs, but they belong to the "that" clause.

D.why: You probably saw the dashes earlier in the sentence and thought this one closes the interruption. That pair already closed after "for instance." A third dash would come between the subject and its verb, and it can't be read as a colon-style dash either, because the text before it is not a complete sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Under its new mobility plan, the city of Harlow Bay no longer measures access by distance alone. Surveyors now record both how long, in minutes rather than miles, a resident needs to reach the nearest grocery store, clinic, or ______ many of those destinations the resident can reach without a car. Planners argue that the second figure reveals inequities the first one conceals.
explanation: The verb "record" takes one object built on the pair "both ... and": both how long a resident needs to reach the nearest grocery store, clinic, or park, and how many destinations the resident can reach without a car. The words "in minutes rather than miles" are an interruption that opens and closes with commas, so nothing is left open by the time you reach the blank. The list "grocery store, clinic, or park" also finishes with "park." At the blank, "and" joins two parallel "how" phrases. Neither phrase can stand alone as a sentence, and "both ... and" should never be split by punctuation. "Park and how" keeps the pair together.

A.why: This catches you because of all the commas just before it. A comma looks like it carries on the series in "grocery store, clinic, or park," or seems to set off a long first item. But that list ends at "park," and "and" here joins two "how" phrases that aren't clauses, under "both ... and." No comma goes between paired items that aren't clauses.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. Neither "Surveyors now record both how long ... park" (the "both" has no matching "and") nor "and how many of those destinations..." can stand alone as a sentence.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so the text before it must be a complete sentence. Here it isn't, because "both" is waiting for its "and." The dash also cuts the "both ... and" pair in half, turning the second item into an afterthought when it is half of the object of "record."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When Ravensholm abolished its downtown parking minimums in 2019, critics predicted gridlock. The housing data told a different story. Developers who had once been required to pair every new apartment with a garage space—a mandate that local builders estimated added about $40,000 to the cost of each unit—______ plans for nearly twice as many apartments over the next two years.
explanation: Cross out the interruption between the dashes, and the sentence reads: "Developers who had once been required to pair every new apartment with a garage space quickly submitted plans..." The subject is "Developers", and the verb is "submitted". The pair of dashes is already complete because the second dash comes right after "unit". Nothing else is needed, and nothing may separate the subject from its verb.

A.why: You took a breath after the long subject and put a comma between "Developers" and its verb "submitted". A comma never separates a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.

C.why: You saw dashes nearby and reached for another one. But the dash after "unit" already closed the interruption. A third dash breaks the sentence between its subject and its verb.

D.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. Everything before the blank is a subject with no verb, so this choice leaves a fragment on both sides.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: After the 2021 floods, hydrologists in the Tessaro Basin installed pressure sensors in a network of shallow wells. They hoped to learn how quickly meltwater, once it had cleared the dense clay of the upper soil, moved through the gravel layer below ______ how long it remained there before reaching the wells that supply the valley's farms.
explanation: The verb "learn" has two parallel objects: "how quickly meltwater... moved through the gravel layer below it" and "how long it remained there". Neither one is a complete sentence. Each is a clause that serves as an object. Two coordinated parts like these are joined by "and" with no punctuation. The comma pair around "once it had cleared the dense clay of the upper soil" is already closed, so the blank has nothing left to close.

A.why: The first object is long, and it already contains commas, so a comma before "and" felt natural. But "and" joins two "how" clauses that are both objects of "learn", not two sentences. A comma does not belong between paired parts.

B.why: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on each side. "How long it remained there..." is not a sentence, and neither is the text before the blank once you remove the main clause "They hoped to learn".

D.why: You may have thought an interruption still needed closing. The commas around "once it had cleared..." already form a complete pair. A lone dash here cuts the second object off from the verb it belongs to.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: For three winters the Hallam regional forecast model overpredicted freezing rain by a wide margin. Its developers first suspected the model's temperature data, then its handling of mountain terrain. The error was finally traced to a single, rarely examined assumption about how quickly frozen ground releases its stored cold ______ been copied unchanged from a version of the model written in 1994.
explanation: The clause "that had been copied unchanged..." identifies which assumption caused the error, so it is essential to the meaning. An essential clause beginning with "that" attaches directly to the noun it describes, with no punctuation. The long phrase between "assumption" and "that" does not change this. The clause still modifies "assumption".

A.why: The noun phrase is long, and there is already a comma in "single, rarely examined", so you added a pause. A comma never comes before an essential "that" clause. The earlier comma joins two adjectives and does not need a partner.

C.why: A semicolon requires a complete sentence after it. "That had been copied unchanged..." is a relative clause with no main clause of its own, so this choice leaves a fragment.

D.why: A dash would set the clause off as an add-on, but a "that" clause cannot be set off by punctuation. It has to stay attached to the noun it identifies. A single dash also suggests an interruption that never closes.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Marine engineers have long sought a hull coating that repels barnacles and resists salt corrosion without leaching copper into the water. A silicone-based coating developed at Brennholt University may be the first to succeed. Its final trials, run in a chamber that cycled between freezing brine and tropical humidity every six hours, ______ resistance to corrosion that no copper-free coating had previously matched.
explanation: Remove the interruption between the commas, and the core sentence is "Its final trials demonstrated a resistance to corrosion..." "Demonstrated" is a verb, and "a resistance" is its object. Nothing separates a verb from its object. The comma after "hours" already closed the interruption.

A.why: You may have seen "a resistance..." as the thing being revealed and reached for a colon. But a colon needs a complete sentence before it. "Its final trials... demonstrated" is unfinished, because "demonstrated" still needs its object.

B.why: After a long subject with commas around it, you added another pause. A comma between a verb and its direct object is never correct.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so the text before it must be a complete sentence, and it is not. The dash also separates "demonstrated" from its object.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sketches recovered from a Lisbon bookseller's attic in 2018 have changed how scholars date Inês Carvalho's String Quartet No. 2. The pages show that Carvalho revised both the tempo markings she had crossed out and rewritten three times in the slow movement ______ entire closing fugue, a section long attributed to one of her students.
explanation: "Both... and" joins two parallel objects of "revised": "the tempo markings she had crossed out and rewritten three times in the slow movement" and "the entire closing fugue". The two parts of a paired construction are joined by "and" alone, with no punctuation. The comma before "a section long attributed..." comes later and belongs to the appositive, not to this junction.

B.why: The first object is long and contains its own "and", so a comma before the second "and" felt like a helpful pause. In a "both... and" pair, no comma separates the two parts.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "And the entire closing fugue..." is a noun phrase, not a sentence, so this choice creates a fragment.

D.why: A dash here treats the second object as an afterthought. That breaks the "both... and" pair, which has to read as one unbroken structure.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a twelve-week trial at the Ostrava Metabolic Institute, 240 adults followed identical calorie targets but were randomly assigned to eat their largest meal either at breakfast or at dinner. The results surprised the researchers themselves. Whether participants ate their largest meal early or late in the day ______ less to their weight change than how much protein that meal contained.
explanation: There is no other subject after the blank, so the whole "whether" clause, "Whether participants ate their largest meal early or late in the day", is the subject of the verb "mattered". It is not an introductory clause. A subject and its verb are never separated by punctuation.

A.why: You applied the rule that an introductory clause takes a comma, as in "Whether they ate early or late, participants lost weight." But no subject follows the blank, so the "whether" clause is itself the subject. A comma would split it from its verb.

B.why: A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides. The "whether" clause has no main verb of its own, and "mattered less..." has no subject.

C.why: A single dash works like a colon, so the text before it must be a complete sentence, and the "whether" clause is not one. The dash also cuts the subject off from its verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before allowing the Kestrel Gorge Dam to return to full reservoir levels, state engineers required a year of continuous monitoring of the structure. Strain gauges, tiltmeters, and acoustic sensors embedded along the dam's patched downstream ______ no movement greater than a tenth of a millimeter in any of the twelve months.
explanation: The subject is the whole list, "Strain gauges, tiltmeters, and acoustic sensors", plus the phrase that describes them, "embedded along the dam's patched downstream face". The verb is "recorded". The commas inside the list separate list items and do not open an interruption that needs closing. No punctuation goes between the subject and its verb.

B.why: The commas in the list made the subject look like it needed a closing comma, as if it were an interruption. Those commas only separate list items. A comma at the blank would split the subject from its verb.

C.why: A dash here treats the long subject as a lead-in to something else. Nothing earlier opened with a dash, and a dash cannot separate a subject from its verb.

D.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. The text before the blank is a subject with no verb, and the text after it is a verb with no subject.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cover crops planted after harvest are widely credited with returning nitrogen to the soil, but few studies have followed that nitrogen into the next season's crop. Over four seasons on 46 test plots, agronomists at the Lindqvist Field Station ______ much nitrogen each cover crop released and how much of it the following corn crop actually absorbed.
explanation: "Measured" is a verb, and its object is the pair of clauses "how much nitrogen each cover crop released and how much of it the following corn crop actually absorbed". A verb and its object are never separated by punctuation. The comma after "plots" ends the introductory phrase, and it does not call for another mark later.

A.why: The long object made you want a pause after the verb. A comma never separates a verb from its object, even when the object is a long "how" clause.

B.why: You saw two "how" clauses and treated them like a list a colon introduces. But a colon needs a complete sentence before it, and "agronomists... measured" is unfinished without its object.

C.why: A single dash follows the same rule as a colon: the text before it must be a complete sentence, and it is not. The dash also separates "measured" from its object.
